Employer shares and your paycheque: stress both sources of household risk

Four charts combine a fall in employer-share value with interrupted earnings, then trace accessible cash, bill dates and an independently assumed sale.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Stress employer shares and take-home income together

Interactive planning lab

Immediate loss on employer shares$24,000
Unfunded bills while keeping the shares$10,000
Unfunded bills after the assumed net-cash sale$0

Hypothetical joint stress, not a prediction of a company’s shares, employment or benefit eligibility. The employer-share shock occurs immediately before month one; other investment values stay fixed as a control. Both paths receive the same household income schedule and essential bills over twelve months. The hold path sells nothing. The sale path assumes all entered shares are vested, saleable and sold immediately after the shock; only the independently entered usable percentage of gross value enters cash. The remainder is excluded from spending, without calculating tax, gains, withholding or fees. Any real tax shortfall must be funded separately. Unvested awards, options, blackout restrictions and future awards are outside this model. Bills arrive at the start of each month; net income arrives at month-end. Bills can use only accessible cash then available. Unfunded amounts remain recorded separately, without automatic debt or retroactive payment from later income. Cash earns no interest. The comparison neither sells other investments nor values the long-term benefits of continuing to hold shares.

The central idea

An employer can affect both the assets you own and the income you use for bills. Test those channels together before counting company shares as a cash reserve.

01

One company can appear on both sides of the plan

An employee holding company shares has two different exposures to the same organisation: the market value of an investment and the cash income from employment. A weak company outcome can put both under pressure. Looking only at the investment account can miss the dependence of the household budget on the same business.

The SEC’s investor bulletin on ten investing principles identifies employer stock as a particular concentration concern because investment losses can coincide with losing employment. That is the reason for testing a joint stress. It does not establish how likely the combination is for a specific company or employee.

This tool deliberately combines an immediate share-price fall with an interruption in take-home earnings. It does not model a named issuer, estimate a default probability or infer a relationship from historical data. The values and dates are editable assumptions chosen to expose the mechanics of a cash plan.

02

Separate the asset loss from the loss of recurring income

The first chart isolates the employer-share loss. In the original example, CAD 60,000 of shares falls by 40%, leaving CAD 36,000 and a CAD 24,000 asset-value loss. The initial CAD 12,000 of accessible cash and CAD 140,000 of other financial investments remain unchanged in this controlled comparison.

Holding other assets unchanged is a modelling control, not a claim that they would be protected in a downturn. A more extensive stress could also reduce their prices, examine fund overlap and change the time required to access them. They are intentionally not sold to rescue the cash ledger here.

Only existing vested, saleable shares belong in the share-value field. An unvested award, an option exercise opportunity and a share already owned are different rights. Future awards should not be counted as money already available. This model does not establish vesting, continued employment conditions, sale permission or the value of employee options.

03

A monthly income figure still needs a receipt date

The cash ledger lasts twelve months. Each month’s essential bill comes first; income arrives at month-end. During the selected interruption, the household receives the separately entered net replacement cash. Afterwards it receives the normal take-home amount. The same schedule applies to both share-holding alternatives.

With CAD 4,000 of monthly essentials, CAD 1,000 of replacement cash and a six-month interruption, the original hold-shares example accumulates CAD 10,000 of unfunded bills. Some of that gap occurs in month seven: the first resumed CAD 6,000 pay receipt still arrives after that month’s bill. Annual totals alone would conceal this timing problem.

The second chart shows cash after the bill and before income. A zero point can indicate exhausted cash, with part of the bill still unpaid. The third chart retains those unpaid amounts separately. Later salary does not retrospectively make an earlier payment timely, and the model does not automatically add a loan or assume that a creditor will wait.

04

A possible share sale is a separate access and tax question

The alternative assumes all entered company shares are sold immediately after the initial price shock. The selected usable percentage converts gross market value into independently assumed net spending cash. It can allow for money held back for tax or costs, but it does not calculate either.

At the original 40% share-price fall and 90% usable percentage, CAD 32,400 enters accessible cash. That makes the initial spending pool CAD 44,400. It funds every requested bill in the original twelve-month example. The remaining share value is excluded from spending and is not treated as a calculated tax liability or refund.

This assumption can fail if shares are restricted, the market is illiquid, settlement is delayed, or a sale is not permitted. Before using sale proceeds in a real cash calendar, verify the actual terms and the separately estimated tax obligation. The chart is not an instruction to sell and does not value the longer-term opportunity of holding the shares.

05

Use the matrix to test dependence rather than predict an event

The fourth chart varies the share-price loss and the length of the income interruption. Every cell uses the assumed immediate-sale path, with the selected usable-cash percentage, opening reserve, income amounts and essential bills. A larger share loss reduces what a sale can contribute to the reserve.

The rows are stresses, not probabilities. The columns are durations, not forecasts of time needed to find work. Even the zero-interruption column needs enough opening cash for the first bill because ordinary pay arrives afterwards. If the replacement amount exceeds normal income, a longer interruption can improve cash in this model; the tool preserves that input rather than assuming a direction.

  1. List the employer-linked assets and distinguish vested holdings from contingent awards.
  2. Identify cash accessible independently of the employer.
  3. Draw the dates of bills and independently confirmed net income receipts.
  4. Test a share loss and an earnings interruption in the same calendar.
  5. Resolve every unfunded payment and verify sale restrictions and tax before implementation.

Those steps connect portfolio concentration with household resilience. The result is a funding test, not an allocation recommendation or an estimate of job-loss risk.
